evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.1.note: Centuries are written with KEY_TERMS' pattern for 'the 1400s' (ช่วงปี 1400): 'late 700s to early 900s' = ปลายช่วงปี 700 ถึงต้นช่วงปี 900, '900s to 1100s' = ช่วงปี 900 ถึงช่วงปี 1100. This keeps the checker's numbers, but คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 8–10 is what Thai history books say. A reviewer should decide one style for the whole course. Second pass, one style for centuries across the course: one century is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 (KEY_TERMS); a run of two or more is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1800 กว่า ("1400 to 1800-something": accurate to the end of the last century and keeps the English numbers for the checker); late/early is ปลายช่วงปี 700 ถึง 799 / ต้นช่วงปี 900 ถึง 999; picture labels and year labels use a dash (ช่วงปี 1400–1499). Where the English itself says '15th century' (teachers' notes, picture alt) the Thai keeps คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 15 next to the years. ช่วงปี 1400 alone (which reads as 'around 1400') and ช่วงปีคริสต์ศักราช 700 กว่า are gone. A native speaker should confirm กว่า reads well.

read.sections.0.text.source: Butuan is a city on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines, close to rivers and the sea. In the 1970s and 1980s, archaeologists studied old wooden boats there, called balangay. The National Museum of the Philippines says the boats were built from planks, joined using a method called lashed-lug. It says they were built between the late 700s and the early 900s. The planks are maritime evidence: people here built boats for travel by water. But they do not record who sailed, what they carried or where they went. A line on a map from Butuan to another island would show a possible link, not a proven trip.
read.sections.0.text.note: balangay = บาลังไกย์ (glossary word), the spelling the course text and section checks use; Thai sources also write บาลังไก or บาลาไง. 'Chinese wares' = เครื่องถ้วยจีน (the usual Thai term for Chinese ceramics), 'blue-and-white wares' = เครื่องลายคราม.
read.sections.0.text.back: Butuan is a city on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines, near a river and the sea. In the 1970s and 1980s, archaeologists studied old wooden boats there called balangay boats. The National Museum of the Philippines says these boats were built from planks, fastened together with a method called lug-lashing. The museum says the boats were built between the late 700s and the early 900s. These planks are maritime evidence: people here built boats to travel by water. But the planks do not record who sailed the boats, what they carried or where they went. So a line on a map from Butuan to other islands shows a possible connection, not a proven journey.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Butuan is a city in the Philippines. It is near the sea. Archaeologists found old wooden boats there. These boats are called balangay. Each boat was made of long, flat pieces of wood. They were built more than 1,000 years ago. The boats are maritime evidence. They show that people built boats to travel by water. But they do not show who sailed. They do not show where the boats went.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Butuan is a city in the Philippines. It is near the sea. Archaeologists found old wooden boats there. These boats are called balangay. Each boat was made from long flat planks. The boats were built more than 1,000 years ago. These boats are maritime evidence. The boats tell us people built boats to travel by water. But the boats do not tell who sailed them, and do not tell where they went.

read.sections.1.text.source: The National Museum in Butuan also shows other finds from the area. Many were dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s. The museum says they point to early trade with China and other parts of Southeast Asia. Another museum article says graves in the wider Butuan and Surigao area held many Chinese wares, or pottery. Many were made in the 900s to 1100s, and some later. These objects were imported: made in one place and brought to another. The pottery and the boats are different finds, often from a different time and context. We can use both to ask about links across the sea. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.
read.sections.1.text.back: The National Museum in Butuan also shows other objects found in this area. Many were dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s. The museum says these objects point to early trade with China and other parts of Southeast Asia. Another museum article says graves in the area around Butuan and Surigao held many Chinese wares, or Chinese pottery. Many were made in the 900s to 1100s, and some were made after that. These objects are imported: made in one place and brought to another place. The pottery and the boats are different finds, and often come from different times and different contexts. We can use both to ask questions about connections across the sea, but no one found pottery inside the boats.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The museum in Butuan has other old things too. Some came from China. They were imported. That means they were made in one place and brought to another. Chinese pottery was found in graves near Butuan. Much of it is from the 900s to the 1100s. Some is later. The pottery and the boats are different finds. Each has its own context and date. We can use both as clues. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: The museum in Butuan has other old things too. Some came from China. These things are imported. That means made in one place, then brought to another place. People found Chinese pottery in graves near Butuan. Many pieces are from the 900s to the 1100s. Some is from later than that. The pottery and the boats are different finds. Each has its own context and date. We can use both as clues, but no one found pottery inside the boats.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of old balangay planks in the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan. It was taken in 2015, more than 1,000 years after the boats were built. Look at the shape of the wood and the round holes along it. The photo supports one claim: people in Butuan built boats from wooden planks. A bigger claim, that people in the region were linked by sea, needs more clues, such as imported objects. The photo alone cannot show the route of this boat. It also cannot tell us if trade was always fair or peaceful.
read.sections.2.text.note: 'Balangay Shrine Museum' = พิพิธภัณฑ์บาลังไกย์ชไรน์ in the reading (read aloud) and kept as Balangay Shrine Museum in the evidence and caption. Check whether a Thai name is used.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo of old planks of a balangay boat in the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan. It was taken in 2015, more than 1,000 years after the boat was built. Look at the shape of the wood and the round holes lined up along the planks. This photo supports one claim: people in Butuan built boats from planks. The bigger claim that people in this region were connected by sea needs more clues, such as imported objects. One photo cannot show this boat's route, and cannot tell either whether trade was always fair or peaceful.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: The second picture is a photo of old pieces of a boat. They are in a museum in Butuan. The photo is from 2015. Can you see the holes in the wood? The photo shows that people built boats from wood. We need more clues to show links by sea. Imported things are one clue. The photo does not show where this boat went. It does not show if trade was fair.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The second picture is a photo of old pieces of a boat. These pieces are in a museum in Butuan. The photo was taken in 2015. Can you see the holes in the planks? The photo tells us people built boats from wood. We need more clues to say people were connected by sea. Imported things are one clue. The photo does not say where this boat went, and does not say whether trade was fair.

Chinese pottery was found in graves nearby. These clues are different because they are separate finds. Much of the pottery is later than the boats. We cannot yet say where the boat in the photo went. Another source that could help is a record from a port across the sea.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Many of the imported wares come from graves, and some finds were dug up by treasure hunters. The lesson says so plainly, without detail; keep the focus on objects and dates. Exchange across the sea was not always fair or peaceful, but the lesson makes no claim either way. Never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys by sea, home countries, religion or ethnicity.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Many imported wares came from graves, and some finds were dug up by treasure hunters. The lesson says so directly without going into detail; keep the focus on objects and dates. Exchange across the sea was not always fair or peaceful, but the lesson makes no claim either way. Do not ask learners about their own or their family's sea journeys, home country, religion or ethnicity.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners make a two-clue claim about links across the sea and name what the evidence cannot show. Evidence move: put the boats' date (late 700s to early 900s) and the imported wares' dates (many 900s–1100s, some 1200s–1300s) in two separate boxes on the board before anyone links them. A sound answer uses two clues for wider contacts without claiming one voyage or one deposit.
educatorNotes.0.back: Goal: learners make a claim from two clues about connections across the sea and can say what the evidence cannot show. Evidence skill: write the boats' date (late 700–799 to early 900–999) and the imported wares' date (many 900–1100-something, some 1200–1300-something) in two separate boxes on the board before anyone links the two. A good answer uses two clues to talk about broad contact, without claiming a single voyage or a single deposit.

educatorNotes.1.source: Misconceptions to address: the planks in the photo are not dated to the same context as every other object, and the wares were not found in a boat. The National Museum's 2022 maritime article mentions Changsha ceramics from Mt Kamhantik in Mulanay (Quezon) and from Laurel (Batangas), not from Butuan; Butuan's own evidence is the Butuan gallery and the grave finds of the wider Agusan del Norte and Surigao del Sur area. Source caveat: published dates for the boats differ. The 2022 article gives the late 8th to early 10th centuries, while UNESCO's 2006 Tentative List entry (submitted by the National Museum) gives the 10th to 13th centuries; that difference is itself a good example of evidence being revised.
educatorNotes.1.back: Misconceptions to address: the planks in the photo are not dated as coming from the same context as every other object, and the wares were not found in the boats. The National Museum's 2022 maritime article discusses Changsha pottery from Mt Kamhantik in Mulanay (Quezon) and from Laurel (Batangas), not from Butuan. Butuan's own evidence is the gallery in Butuan and grave finds in Agusan del Norte and Surigao del Sur. Source caution: the published dates for the boats differ. The 2022 article gives the late 8th to early 10th centuries, while the 2006 UNESCO Tentative List entry (put forward by the National Museum) gives the 10th to 13th centuries (years 900 to 1200-something). This difference is a good example of revising evidence.
